Vaccination Timeliness

PAHO/CIM

October 8, 2026

Source: vignettes/articles/en/vaccination_timeliness_en.Rmd
vaccination_timeliness_en.Rmd

🌐 Lea esto en español

Rationale

A country’s immunization schedule is established taking into account the characteristics of each vaccine, the natural history of the disease it aims to prevent, the characteristics of the person who will receive it, the population’s access to vaccination sites, and their willingness to get vaccinated (or to have their children vaccinated).

Vaccination aims to reduce the greatest possible burden of disease by acting ahead of the period of life in which the risk of severe illness and death from that disease is highest. At the same time, the schedule must consider the vaccine’s capacity to generate immunity and the duration of that immunity, which is conditioned (especially during the first year of life) by the maturity of the immune system. These factors determine, for example, the need for more than one dose, booster doses throughout the life course, the compatibility of vaccines administered simultaneously, and the minimum intervals between doses.

To obtain the greatest benefit from the schedule established by the health authorities, compliance by the population is essential, not only by completing the schedule, but by doing so in a timely manner. Knowing vaccination timeliness, that is, how closely vaccines are administered according to the schedule, allows us to:

  • understand coverage and its impact on the epidemiology of the disease,
  • monitor the supply chain of vaccines and supplies,
  • investigate access problems or willingness to vaccinate in certain communities, and
  • through actions at different levels, prevent future dropouts.

Therefore, the objective of this indicator is to analyze vaccination timeliness in the population, that is, the time that elapses between the age of eligibility for a given vaccine dose and the occurrence of the vaccination, using nominal data from Electronic Immunization Registries (EIR).

Note

  1. All functions used for vaccination timeliness analyses within PAHOabc begin with the vt_ prefix.

Non-probabilistic Analysis

The non-probabilistic analysis measures the time that elapses between the age indicated for a given dose and its administration. It is based on the database of vaccinated individuals in the EIR, so it is measured retrospectively over the total number of individuals who received the dose. It estimates the proportion of individuals who receive the vaccine in a timely manner and the proportion who receive it in an untimely manner. Those who did not receive the vaccine in a timely manner are then stratified according to the time elapsed outside the timeliness window.

Operational Definitions

  • Timely vaccination: vaccination administered within the time range defined by the country as the timeliness standard for each dose of a vaccine.
  • Percentage of timely vaccination: proportion of the population that received a dose within its timeliness window, out of the total population that received that dose.
  • Distribution by time elapsed (delay): stratification of the individuals who did not receive the dose in a timely manner, distributed into time categories defined by the country.

Required Definitions

Before carrying out the analysis, the country must define:

  • Vaccines to evaluate: each vaccine dose is analyzed individually. An aggregated analysis of several doses can then be carried out.
  • Timeliness per vaccine: for each dose, the period considered timely is defined, with a minimum and a maximum age, according to the country’s guidelines. In PAHOabc, this period corresponds to the age_schedule_low and age_schedule_high columns of the vaccination schedule.
  • Time categories: ranges of days used to distribute untimely vaccinations. The country defines the ranges, although the package includes predefined ranges.
  • Year to evaluate: it is up to the country to analyze by birth cohort or by calendar year. The vt_ functions allow filtering by birth cohort with the birth_cohorts parameter.
  • Level of geographic disaggregation: national (ADM0), first subnational level (ADM1), or second subnational level (ADM2).
  • Minimum observation period: each individual included in the analysis must have at least completed the timeliness window of the dose being evaluated.

Warning

PAHOabc does not verify the minimum observation period. If birth cohorts that have not yet completed the timeliness window by the date the data were extracted are included, only those already vaccinated will appear in the EIR, which overestimates timeliness. Choose birth_cohorts that have had enough time to complete the timeliness window of the doses analyzed.

Characteristics of the Analysis

  • It is a cross-sectional analysis: the number of days between the date of birth and the date of administration of the dose is measured and compared with the timeliness standard defined by the country. If the age at vaccination falls within the timeliness window, the dose is classified as timely; if it falls before or after it, it is classified as untimely.
  • It is independent of the size of the target population: the denominator is all individuals who received the dose being evaluated.
  • It requires the vaccination schedule with the specification of the timeliness standard.
  • It uses the place of residence for subnational analyses.

Calculation of the Indicator

The timely vaccination indicator is calculated as:

Timely vaccination (%)=Doses of vaccine X administered in a timely mannerTotal doses of vaccine X administered in a given period and place×100 \text{Timely vaccination (\%)} = \frac{\text{Doses of vaccine X administered in a timely manner}}{\text{Total doses of vaccine X administered in a given period and place}} \times 100

The distribution of untimely doses by time range is calculated as:

Untimely doses in range A (%)=Untimely doses in range ATotal untimely doses in a given period and place×100 \text{Untimely doses in range A (\%)} = \frac{\text{Untimely doses in range A}}{\text{Total untimely doses in a given period and place}} \times 100

Probabilistic Analysis

The probabilistic analysis estimates the cumulative incidence of the event “administration of a vaccine dose”, that is, the probability that a given population receives the dose as time goes by (from the moment it becomes eligible to receive it). From this curve, the probability of being vaccinated in a timely manner and the time needed to vaccinate different percentiles of the population are estimated.

Note

Ideally, this analysis considers the entire population that should receive the vaccine (for example, from the live birth registry). PAHOabc works with the database of vaccinated individuals in the EIR, that is, only with the individuals who received the dose analyzed. In this case, the final probability will always be 100%, which overestimates the real probability of vaccination of the population.

Operational Definitions

  • Timely vaccination: as in the non-probabilistic analysis, vaccination administered within the timeliness window defined by the country for each dose. In this analysis, day 0 (start of the observation period) corresponds to the lower limit of the timeliness window (age_schedule_low), and doses administered before that day are not included.
  • Probability of being vaccinated by day t: cumulative incidence of vaccination by day t. When t corresponds to the upper limit of the timeliness window, the probability of the population being vaccinated in a timely manner is obtained.
  • Time needed to vaccinate a percentage of the population: number of days from the start of the timeliness window that it takes to vaccinate a given percentile of the population (for example, 25%, 50% and 75%).

Required Definitions

  • Vaccines to evaluate: each dose is analyzed individually, since each one has its own timeliness window.
  • Timeliness per vaccine: same as in the non-probabilistic analysis (between age_schedule_low and age_schedule_high).
  • Population percentiles: it is recommended to estimate at least the times for 25%, 50% and 75%.
  • Year to evaluate: using a birth cohort is suggested. PAHOabc also allows combining several cohorts (see the warning below).
  • Level of geographic disaggregation: ADM0, ADM1 or ADM2.

Warning

This analysis follows the vaccination curve well beyond the timeliness window, so the observation period needed is longer. If birth cohorts that have not completed that observation period by the date the data were extracted are included, only those vaccinated before that date will appear in the EIR. Those vaccinated afterwards do not appear yet, so the curve may show faster vaccination than is really the case. To mitigate this, choose birth cohorts that have completed the observation period, or exclude incomplete cohorts.

Characteristics of the Analysis

  • It is a cumulative incidence analysis, which corresponds to the complement of the Kaplan-Meier survival function. Kaplan-Meier estimates the probability that an event does not happen over time; its complement gives the probability that it does happen, in this case, vaccination.
  • Time is counted from the moment the individual becomes eligible for the dose (from age_schedule_low). All those vaccinated up to the upper limit of the timeliness window are considered timely.
  • It is independent of the size of the population: the denominator is the total number of records included in the analysis.
  • It requires the vaccination schedule with the definition of the timeliness window of each dose.
  • It uses the place of residence for subnational analyses.

Calculation of the Indicator

The cumulative incidence of vaccination by day t is the complement of the Kaplan-Meier survival function:

F(t)=1−S(t) F(t) = 1 - S(t)

where F(t)F(t) is the probability of having been vaccinated by day t and S(t)S(t) is the probability of not having been vaccinated by day t. Since the EIR only contains vaccinated individuals (there is no censoring), F(t)F(t) is simply the cumulative percentage of records vaccinated by day t:

F(t)(%)=Records vaccinated between day 0 and day tTotal records vaccinated from day 0 onwards×100 F(t) \;(\%) = \frac{\text{Records vaccinated between day 0 and day t}}{\text{Total records vaccinated from day 0 onwards}} \times 100

Note

Records vaccinated before the timeliness window (before day 0) and those with a missing date are excluded from both the numerator and the denominator, and are reported separately. Therefore, F(t)F(t) evaluated on the last day of the timeliness window is not equal to the TIMELY percentage of vt_rate(), which does include those vaccinated before the window in its denominator.

Glossary

Political Geographic Boundaries

Throughout this vignette, we will make reference to different levels of political geographic boundaries. These levels are defined by the country/territory and can have different names from country to country. PAHOabc is agnostic to these names and requires the user to recode their variable names to fit the PAHOabc structure.

Namely, PAHOabc can distinguish three administrative levels, which listed from top to bottom level are: ADM0, ADM1 and ADM2.

  1. ADM0: The country. This is the top-most administrative level.
  2. ADM1: The first geographic subdivision in the country. ADM0 contains several ADM1 subdivisions.
  3. ADM2: The second geographic subdivision in the country. Each ADM1 contains several ADM2 subdivisions.

Timeliness Categories

Category Meaning
TIMELY The age at vaccination falls within [age_schedule_low, age_schedule_high].
UNTIMELY_EARLY The age at vaccination is lower than age_schedule_low (before the timeliness window).
UNTIMELY_LATE The age at vaccination is greater than age_schedule_high (after the timeliness window).
DATE_MISSING date_vax or date_birth is NA.

Usage

Install Package 

devtools::install_github("IM-Data-PAHO/pahoabc")

Load Data

The functions in this module require your EIR dataset and a vaccination schedule with the timeliness windows, both in the standard PAHOabc format.

EIR

The pahoabc::pahoabc.EIR data frame provides a simulated, nominal-level table representing individual vaccination events from an EIR. Each row corresponds to a single vaccination act for a person.

pahoabc.EIR %>% head() %>% kable(caption = "Example Electronic Immunization Registry")
Example Electronic Immunization Registry
ID date_birth date_vax ADM1_residence ADM2_residence ADM1_occurrence ADM2_occurrence dose
191997 2023-08-08 2023-12-26 ADM1_4 ADM2_4_35 ADM1_4 ADM2_4_35 DTP2
212189 2023-12-20 2023-12-26 ADM1_5 ADM2_5_61 ADM1_5 ADM2_5_61 BCG RN
118063 2022-09-15 2023-12-26 ADM1_2 ADM2_2_5 ADM1_2 ADM2_2_5 DTP1
118063 2022-09-15 2023-12-26 ADM1_2 ADM2_2_5 ADM1_2 ADM2_2_5 YFV1
130751 2022-10-27 2023-12-12 ADM1_5 ADM2_5_55 ADM1_5 ADM2_5_55 YFV1
136532 2021-09-21 2023-12-26 ADM1_3 ADM2_3_12 ADM1_3 ADM2_3_12 SRP1
  • ID: Unique person identification number.
  • date_birth: Date of birth of person.
  • date_vax: Date of vaccination event.
  • ADM1_residence / ADM2_residence: First and second geographic administrative levels of residence.
  • dose: Combined variable representing vaccine type and dose number (e.g., DTP1).

Warning

  1. The functions in this module calculate age at vaccination as date_vax - date_birth. If data.EIR contains records where date_vax occurs before date_birth (i.e., a negative age at vaccination), this points to a date consistency error. When this happens, vt_ functions will emit a warning directing you to the Date Consistency Comparison module to identify and resolve those records first.
  2. The functions in this module count vaccination records, not individuals. If data.EIR contains duplicate records (the same ID and dose registered more than once), that individual is counted more than once in both the numerator and the denominator. PAHOabc does not remove duplicates, so make sure to remove them before running the analysis. Note that it is up to you to decide which record to keep for each ID and dose (e.g., the one with the earliest date_vax).

Vaccination Schedule

The pahoabc::pahoabc.schedule dataset defines the national immunization schedule, listing for each vaccine dose its age of administration and its timeliness window, in days.

pahoabc.schedule %>% kable(caption = "Example Immunization Schedule with timeliness windows")
Example Immunization Schedule with timeliness windows
dose age_schedule age_schedule_low age_schedule_high
SRP1 365 360 420
DTP1 60 54 90
DTP2 120 116 150
DTP3 180 176 210
BCG RN 0 0 28
YFV1 365 360 420
  • dose: Combined variable representing vaccine type and dose number.
  • age_schedule: The age of administration of the corresponding dose, in days.
  • age_schedule_low: The minimum age of the timeliness window, in days.
  • age_schedule_high: The maximum age of the timeliness window, in days.

For example, in this schedule DTP1 is indicated at 60 days of age and is considered timely if administered between 54 and 90 days of age.

Non-probabilistic Analysis

Expected Workflow

The functions for the non-probabilistic analysis are:

  1. vt_rate(): computes the percentage of timely vaccination, pooled across several doses or disaggregated by dose, and by geographic level.
  2. vt_barplot(): visualizes the output of vt_rate() as a stacked bar chart.
  3. vt_inconsistent(): lists individual untimely and missing-date records, also indicating the number of days outside the timeliness window.
  4. vt_inconsistent_plot(): visualizes the distribution of untimely doses by the number of days outside the timeliness window.
Figure 1. Expected workflow for the non-probabilistic section of the vaccination timeliness analysis.


Note

  1. The examples below analyze the 2022 birth cohort. The example data includes vaccinations up to December 31, 2023, so this cohort has completed the timeliness window of the doses administered during the first year of life.
  2. Filtering by birth_cohorts excludes records with no date of birth, so in that case DATE_MISSING only counts records missing the date of vaccination.

Step 1 — Compute the indicator with vt_rate()

vt_rate() compares the age at vaccination against the timeliness window of each dose and returns the number (n) and percentage (rate) of records that are TIMELY, UNTIMELY_EARLY, UNTIMELY_LATE, or DATE_MISSING, out of the total number of records (total).

By default, vaccines = NULL pools all doses in data.schedule into a single indicator. Here we compute the pooled indicator at the ADM1 level:

rate_df <- vt_rate(
  data.EIR      = pahoabc.EIR,
  data.schedule = pahoabc.schedule,
  geo_level     = "ADM1",
  birth_cohorts = 2022
)

rate_df %>% kable(digits = 2, caption = "Vaccination timeliness pooled by ADM1, 2022 cohort")

Specifying vaccines disaggregates the results by dose:

rate_by_dose_df <- vt_rate(
  data.EIR      = pahoabc.EIR,
  data.schedule = pahoabc.schedule,
  geo_level     = "ADM1",
  vaccines      = c("DTP1", "DTP2", "DTP3"),
  birth_cohorts = 2022
)

rate_by_dose_df %>% head(10) %>% kable(digits = 2, caption = "Vaccination timeliness by dose and ADM1, 2022 cohort")

Parameters accepted
  • data.EIR: EIR data frame in PAHOabc format.
  • data.schedule: Vaccination schedule data frame in PAHOabc format.
  • geo_level: "ADM0" (default), "ADM1", or "ADM2".
  • vaccines: Character vector of doses to include, disaggregating results by dose. Default NULL pools all doses in data.schedule.
  • birth_cohorts: Numeric vector of birth cohort year(s) to include. Default NULL uses all available cohorts.

Step 2 — Visualize the indicator with vt_barplot()

The output of vt_rate() can be passed directly to vt_barplot() to produce a stacked bar chart. If the data is disaggregated by dose, the plot is automatically faceted by dose.

vt_barplot(data = rate_df)

vt_barplot(data = rate_by_dose_df)

Parameters accepted
  • data: Output of vt_rate().
  • within_ADM1: Character vector to filter to specific ADM1 units when geo_level = "ADM2". Default: NULL.
  • plot_missing: Boolean. If TRUE (default), DATE_MISSING records are shown as a separate bar segment so all bars sum to 100%.
Interpretation

Each bar represents a geographic unit and is divided into segments: TIMELY (blue), UNTIMELY_LATE (orange), UNTIMELY_EARLY (purple), and DATE_MISSING (grey). Bars with a larger orange share indicate units where a large share of doses are administered after the timeliness window, a signal worth investigating for possible access, willingness to vaccinate, or supply issues in those units. A large purple share, on the other hand, can point to data entry errors or problems in how the schedule is applied.

Note

No grey segment appears because filtering by the 2022 cohort excluded records with no date of birth, and no records in this cohort are missing the date of vaccination.

Step 3 — Inspect individual untimely records with vt_inconsistent()

vt_inconsistent() returns a record-level table of all UNTIMELY_EARLY, UNTIMELY_LATE and DATE_MISSING doses, including the number of days outside the timeliness window.

Note

In this example we do not filter by birth cohort, because doing so would exclude records with no date of birth.

inconsistent_df <- vt_inconsistent(
  data.EIR      = pahoabc.EIR,
  data.schedule = pahoabc.schedule,
  vaccines      = "DTP1"
)

inconsistent_df %>%
  # shows up to 2 records of each type: UNTIMELY_EARLY, UNTIMELY_LATE and DATE_MISSING
  group_by(timeliness) %>%
  slice_head(n = 2) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  kable(caption = "Sample of untimely and missing-date DTP1 records")
Sample of untimely and missing-date DTP1 records
ID dose date_birth date_vax age_at_vax age_schedule_low age_schedule_high days_outside_range timeliness
71494 DTP1 NA 2022-04-11 NA 54 90 NA DATE_MISSING
86449 DTP1 NA 2022-06-08 NA 54 90 NA DATE_MISSING
90277 DTP1 2022-02-28 2022-03-29 29 54 90 -25 UNTIMELY_EARLY

Parameters accepted
  • data.EIR: EIR data frame in PAHOabc format.
  • data.schedule: Vaccination schedule data frame in PAHOabc format.
  • vaccines: Character vector of doses to include. Default NULL includes all doses in data.schedule.
  • birth_cohorts: Numeric vector of birth cohort year(s) to include. Default NULL uses all available cohorts.

The days_outside_range column is negative when a person was vaccinated before age_schedule_low, and positive when vaccinated after age_schedule_high (NA when a date is missing). This table can be exported for record-level follow-up.

Step 4 — Visualize the distribution by time elapsed with vt_inconsistent_plot()

vt_inconsistent_plot() produces a plot of untimely doses, grouped by the number of days outside the timeliness window. Doses administered after the timeliness window and before it are shown in separate rows, each with its own y-axis scale.

vt_inconsistent_plot(
  data.EIR      = pahoabc.EIR,
  data.schedule = pahoabc.schedule,
  vaccines      = "DTP1",
  birth_cohorts = 2022
)

When more than one vaccine is specified, the plot adds one column per dose. Within each row, all doses share the same scale, so they can be compared with each other:

vt_inconsistent_plot(
  data.EIR      = pahoabc.EIR,
  data.schedule = pahoabc.schedule,
  vaccines      = c("DTP1", "DTP2", "DTP3"),
  birth_cohorts = 2022
)

Parameters accepted
  • data.EIR: EIR data frame in PAHOabc format.
  • data.schedule: Vaccination schedule data frame in PAHOabc format.
  • vaccines: Character vector of doses to include, adding one column per dose. Default NULL pools the results of all doses into a single column.
  • birth_cohorts: Numeric vector of birth cohort year(s) to include. Default NULL uses all available cohorts.
  • day_groups: Defines the categories on the horizontal axis. It is a list of c(lower, upper) numeric pairs defining the lower and upper limits of each category, in days. Categories must start at 0 and be contiguous (each one starts where the previous one ends). The last category always extends to the maximum value in the data and is labeled "X+". Default: 10-day groups from 0 up to 90+ days.

Time categories are defined by each country. For example, to use the categories 0 to 39 days, 40 to 49 days, 50 to 59 days, 60 to 89 days, and 90 days or more:

vt_inconsistent_plot(
  data.EIR      = pahoabc.EIR,
  data.schedule = pahoabc.schedule,
  vaccines      = c("DTP1", "DTP2", "DTP3"),
  birth_cohorts = 2022,
  day_groups    = list(c(0, 40), c(40, 50), c(50, 60), c(60, 90), c(90, 120))
)

Interpretation

The top row represents doses administered after the timeliness window (delay), while the bottom row shows doses administered before the minimum age. Since each row has its own scale, only compare columns within the same row, and use the summary in the plot caption to compare between rows. The distribution of the data will let you assess where delays are concentrated, for example: are the delays only a few days long, or are most of them concentrated in delays of several months? Likewise, doses administered before the minimum age can point to data entry errors or problems in how the schedule is applied.

Probabilistic Analysis

Expected Workflow

The functions for the probabilistic analysis are:

  1. vt_distribution(): computes, for each day since the start of the timeliness window, the percentage of records vaccinated on that day and the cumulative percentage (cumulative incidence). Results are disaggregated by dose and, optionally, by geographic level.
  2. vt_cdf_plot() and vt_pdf_plot(): visualize the output of vt_distribution() as a cumulative incidence curve (similar to a Kaplan-Meier curve) or as a curve of the percentage vaccinated per day, respectively.
  3. vt_percentile(): from the output of vt_distribution(), computes the number of days needed to vaccinate different percentiles of the population.
  4. vt_percentile_plot(): generates visualizations from the output of vt_percentile().
Figure 2. Expected workflow for the probabilistic section of the vaccination timeliness analysis.


Note

As in the non-probabilistic analysis, the examples below analyze the 2022 birth cohort. Since the example data only include vaccinations up to December 31, 2023, very late vaccinations of this cohort are not observed yet.

Step 1 — Compute the distribution with vt_distribution()

vt_distribution() computes the age at vaccination and expresses it as days since the start of the timeliness window (where day 0 corresponds to age_schedule_low). By default, vaccines = NULL includes all doses in data.schedule:

dist_df <- vt_distribution(
  data.EIR      = pahoabc.EIR,
  data.schedule = pahoabc.schedule,
  birth_cohorts = 2022
)

dist_df %>% head(10) %>% kable(digits = 2, caption = "Distribution of vaccinations by day and dose, 2022 cohort")

dist_by_dose_ADM1_df <- vt_distribution(

  geo_level     = "ADM1",

The table contains one row per dose and day (as long as at least one vaccination occurred), with the following columns:

  • dose: the dose.
  • day: days since the start of the timeliness window (from age_schedule_low).
  • n and pdf: number and percentage of records vaccinated on that day.
  • cum_n and cdf: cumulative number and percentage of records vaccinated up to that day (cumulative incidence).
  • n_at_risk: number of records not yet vaccinated at the start of that day (population “at risk”).
  • total: denominator, that is, all records vaccinated from day 0 onwards.
  • n_early: records vaccinated before the timeliness window, excluded from the analysis.
  • n_missing: records with a missing date, excluded from the analysis.
  • window_end: last day of the timeliness window (age_schedule_high - age_schedule_low).
  • age: age at vaccination (in days).
  • age_schedule_low: lower limit of the timeliness window according to data.schedule (in days).
Parameters accepted
  • data.EIR: EIR table in PAHOabc format.
  • data.schedule: Vaccination schedule table in PAHOabc format.
  • geo_level: "ADM0" (default), "ADM1", or "ADM2".
  • vaccines: Character vector with the doses to include.
  • birth_cohorts: Numeric vector with the birth cohort(s) to include. The default NULL uses all available cohorts.

Step 2 — Visualize the distribution with vt_cdf_plot() and vt_pdf_plot()

The output of vt_distribution() can be passed directly to vt_cdf_plot(), which plots the cumulative incidence curve. The percentile parameter adds a line and a label with the number of days needed to reach that percentile:

vt_cdf_plot(data = dist_df, percentile = 50)

The plot is organized in panels by dose and the timeliness window of each one is shaded. By default, x_axis = "absolute", which means that the x-axis shows the age at vaccination (in days). If the data is disaggregated by subnational levels, each geographic area is shown as a thin grey line, which serves as context, and all areas together are shown as a single highlighted line. This way, the plot remains readable even with tens or hundreds of geographic areas:

vt_cdf_plot(data = dist_by_dose_ADM1_df, percentile = 80)

With the highlight parameter you can highlight up to 5 geographic areas in color to compare them with all areas combined:

vt_cdf_plot(data = dist_by_dose_ADM1_df, percentile = 80, highlight = c("ADM1_1", "ADM1_4"))

With x_axis = "relative", the x-axis shows the days since the start of the timeliness window instead, so all panels start at 0, which makes it easier to compare doses with each other:

vt_cdf_plot(data = dist_by_dose_ADM1_df, percentile = 80, x_axis = "relative")

Parameters accepted by vt_cdf_plot()
  • data: Output of vt_distribution().
  • percentile: A single percentile (greater than 0 and at most 100) to highlight in the plot, for all areas combined and for each area in highlight. Default: NULL (none).
  • highlight: Character vector with up to 5 geographic areas (at the geographic level of data) to highlight in color. Only available if the data is disaggregated by ADM1 or ADM2. Default: NULL (none).
  • within_ADM1: Character vector to filter specific ADM1 units when geo_level = "ADM2". Default: NULL.
  • max_days: Maximum number of days since the start of the timeliness window to show on the x-axis. The default (NULL) shows up to the day by which 95% of the records have been vaccinated, so that a few very late vaccinations (or vaccinations with date errors) do not stretch the axis.
  • x_axis: "absolute" (default) shows the age at vaccination (in days); "relative" shows, for each dose, the days elapsed since the start of the timeliness window.

vt_pdf_plot() plots the percentage of records vaccinated on each day (or in a group of days, set by the binwidth parameter), which lets you see when vaccinations are concentrated:

dist_by_dose_ADM0_df <- vt_distribution(
  data.EIR      = pahoabc.EIR,
  data.schedule = pahoabc.schedule,
  vaccines      = c("DTP1", "DTP2", "DTP3"),
  birth_cohorts = 2022
)

vt_pdf_plot(data = dist_by_dose_ADM0_df, percentile = 50, max_days = 150)

vt_pdf_plot(data = dist_by_dose_ADM1_df, binwidth = 7, highlight = "ADM1_1", max_days = 200)

Note

In this last plot with geographic areas, areas with few records can show very high daily percentages. That is why the y-axis is limited to the highlighted lines, and grey lines that exceed that limit are cut.

Parameters accepted by vt_pdf_plot()

It accepts the same parameters as vt_cdf_plot(), and additionally accepts:

  • binwidth: Number of days represented by each point of the curve (for example, 7 to group by week). In the case of geographic areas with few records, larger values could lead to smoother curves. Default: 1.
Interpretation

Both plots are complementary: in the cumulative incidence curve (cdf), curves that rise quickly indicate vaccination close to the start of the timeliness window, while curves that rise slowly, or that have an important stretch to the right of the shaded area, indicate delays. The same can be seen in the curve of the percentage vaccinated per day (pdf), which directly shows the distribution of vaccinations over time.

The caption of both plots indicates how many records were excluded for having been vaccinated before the timeliness window or for having a missing date. A large number of vaccinations before the window can point to data entry errors or problems in how the schedule is applied; to review them, use vt_inconsistent() and vt_inconsistent_plot().

Warning

Remember that, when working only with vaccinated individuals, all curves end at 100%. This does not mean that the entire target population has been vaccinated, but that the analysis was carried out only with records of vaccinated individuals.

Step 3 — Compute the percentiles with vt_percentile()

vt_percentile() takes the output of vt_distribution() and computes, for each percentile, the number of days needed to reach it. The results keep the same disaggregation as vt_distribution() (by dose and geographic level):

vt_percentile(data = dist_df) %>%
  kable(caption = "Days needed to vaccinate 25%, 50% and 75%, by dose, 2022 cohort")

The within_window column indicates whether the percentile is reached within the timeliness window of the dose.

Parameters accepted
  • data: Output of vt_distribution().
  • percentiles: Numeric vector with the percentiles to compute. Default: c(25, 50, 75).
Interpretation

A larger number of days to reach the same percentile indicates later vaccination. For example, if in one geographic area 50% of the records are vaccinated within the first 10 days and in another it takes 40 days, the second one shows delays that warrant investigating possible problems of access, willingness to vaccinate, or supply.

Step 4 — Compare percentiles between geographic areas with vt_percentile_plot()

The output of vt_percentile() can be passed directly to vt_percentile_plot(), which shows one row per geographic area (or per dose, if the data is not disaggregated geographically). Each percentile is drawn as a point, joined by a line from the lowest to the highest percentile. Rows are sorted according to the median (or the closest percentile). Finally, the timeliness window of each dose is shaded.

vt_percentile(data = dist_by_dose_ADM1_df, percentiles = c(25, 50, 75, 90)) %>%
  vt_percentile_plot()

Without geographic disaggregation, one row per dose is shown:

vt_percentile(data = dist_by_dose_ADM0_df, percentiles = c(25, 50, 75, 90)) %>%
  vt_percentile_plot()

When there are many geographic areas (for example, at the ADM2 level), the n_slowest parameter lets you show only the slowest areas:

vt_distribution(
  data.EIR      = pahoabc.EIR,
  data.schedule = pahoabc.schedule,
  # at the ADM2 level there are many geographic areas
  geo_level     = "ADM2",
  vaccines      = c("DTP1", "DTP3"),
  birth_cohorts = 2022
) %>%
  vt_percentile() %>%
  # show only the 15 slowest
  vt_percentile_plot(n_slowest = 15)

Parameters accepted
  • data: Output of vt_percentile().
  • within_ADM1: Character vector to filter specific ADM1 units when geo_level = "ADM2". Default: NULL.
  • n_slowest: Number of geographic areas to show, starting with the slowest. Default: NULL (that is, all).
Interpretation

The areas at the top of the plot are the ones that take the longest to vaccinate half of their records. Points to the right of the shaded area indicate that the percentile is reached outside the timeliness window, and a long line between the lowest and the highest percentile indicates that vaccination is very spread out over time.

Warning

Geographic areas with few records can show extreme percentiles just by chance. Before concluding that a certain geographic area is vaccinating slowly, check its number of records in the total column of vt_percentile().

Summary

This module allows you to estimate the vaccination timeliness indicator from EIR data. In the non-probabilistic analysis, vt_rate() and vt_barplot() return the percentage of timely vaccination with different geographic or dose-level disaggregations; vt_inconsistent() lets you generate a list of the records detected as untimely or missing vaccination/birth dates; and vt_inconsistent_plot() characterizes the distribution of untimely records by days outside the timeliness window.

In the probabilistic analysis, vt_distribution(), vt_cdf_plot() and vt_pdf_plot() describe how vaccinations accumulate as days go by since the start of the timeliness window, vt_percentile() estimates how many days are needed to vaccinate different percentiles of the population, and vt_percentile_plot() lets you visually compare those times between geographic areas.

Together, these tools help immunization programs understand their coverage, identify communities with access problems or low willingness to vaccinate, and guide actions to prevent future dropouts.
